[Amid growing demands](https://jeffries.house.gov/2026/02/04/leaders-jeffries-
and-schumer-deliver-urgent-ice-reform-demands-to-republican-leadership/) by
Democrats to [overhaul U.S. Immigration and Customs
Enforcement](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/democrats-demands-
overhaul-ice-proliferate-minneapolis-shooting-rcna255987) after federal
immigration officials killed two U.S. citizens in Minnesota, Secretary of
Homeland Security Kristi Noem said in early February 2026 that [agents in
Minneapolis will be issued body-worn
cameras](https://apnews.com/article/immigration-enforcement-minneapolis-
secretary-noem-homeland-security-37af4947057e64efee5e43a8f2e018bb).

But can body cameras on federal officials provide the [transparency and
accountability the public is
demanding](https://www.npr.org/2026/01/10/nx-s1-5673229/ice-protests-
minneapolis-portland-renee-good) from agents with ICE and U.S. Customs and
Border Protection?

As [a public policy scholar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/stephanie-lessing/),
I have analyzed the existing body-worn camera policy for ICE agents. And I’ve
compared this policy to dozens of other state and local body camera policies,
in an effort to investigate the [rationales for their
use](https://doi.org/10.1111/soc4.12952).

Whether ICE’s body camera policy can provide transparency and accountability
depends, I believe, on the policy itself and the enforcement of that policy.
ICE’s use of body cameras could improve the agency’s legitimacy in the eyes of
the public.

But as I’ve seen with other police body camera policies, there’s a risk that
camera footage may obscure actual events. It’s also possible that [the
strategic release of footage may undermine
transparency](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/13/magazine/police-body-cameras-
miguel-richards.html).

**Various body camera policies**

Police body cameras were first used in the United States in 2012 by the
[Rialto Police Department in
California](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10940-014-9236-3). By
2020, their use had expanded to over [62% of local law enforcement
agencies](https://www.policeforum.org/assets/BWCdecadelater.pdf), [covering
79% of local police officers
nationwide](https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/lpdppt20st.pdf).

That expansion was, in part, a response to growing criticism over [stop-and-
frisk tactics](https://digitalcommons.sacredheart.edu/cj_fac/30/) – in which
police temporarily detain people for weapons searches when a crime is
suspected – and [police-involved shootings of people of
color](https://scholarship.law.ufl.edu/flr/vol67/iss5/6/).

Body camera policies vary greatly between municipalities. Some policies make
body cameras useful accountability tools, like those of [Parker,
Colorado](https://public.powerdms.com/PARKERPD/documents/67), which uses
cameras for evidence collection and ensuring officer adherence to policy
rather than as surveillance technology.

Others, meanwhile, provide broad discretion for officers to choose when to
activate their body cameras, such as [Colorado Springs’
policy](https://www.bwcscorecard.org/static/policies/2016-03-24%20Colorado%20Springs%20BWC%20Policy.pdf).
Allowing officers to decide when to use their cameras can limit the
availability of evidence.

I believe there are four crucial elements of a body camera policy that can
ensure that ICE agents properly use the technology.

**Activation requirements**

Body camera quality has improved over the past decade. But the battery life of
many models prevents [continuous recording](https://www.digitalallyinc.com/is-
body-camera-battery-life-impeding-your-teams-abilities/) throughout a 10-hour
shift.

Instead, law enforcement officials often [manually activate their body
cameras](https://www.mass.gov/doc/doc-540-body-worn-cameras/download). Thus,
to effectively promote accountability, a strong policy would require ICE
agents to activate their body cameras before they interact with the public.

[A 2016 study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11292-016-9261-3) found that, without
mandatory camera-activation policies, officers often fail to activate their
cameras.

The [current ICE body-worn camera
policy](https://www.ice.gov/doclib/foia/policy/19010.3.pdf), issued in
February 2025, lists enforcement activities that require recording. They
include executing arrest warrants, frisks of individuals and “[responding to
public, unlawful/violent disturbances at ICE
facilities](https://www.ice.gov/doclib/foia/policy/19010.3.pdf).”

But the list does not include mandatory activation during vehicle pursuits or
the transportation of people to detention facilities. Recording inside
detention facilities is strictly prohibited by the policy.

**Deactivation requirements**

As proposed by the [Police Executive Research
Forum](https://www.policeforum.org/assets/BWCdecadelater.pdf), a nonprofit
that promotes policing professionalism, body cameras must continue to record
until an encounter with a member of the public has concluded and agents have
left the scene.

The current [ICE body-worn camera
policy](https://www.ice.gov/doclib/foia/policy/19010.3.pdf) states that agents
“should only deactivate the BWC when the scene is secure as determined by the
supervisor or team leader.”

While robust policies, such as that of the Chicago Police Department, [require
continued recording](https://home.chicagopolice.org/wp-
content/uploads/S03-14_BWC_DRAFT_16NOV22.pdf) during the transportation of
detained people, the ICE body camera policy does not. This creates the
potential for critical moments to go unrecorded.

**Facial recognition**

Many body camera models come equipped with facial recognition technology. But
many [local police department policies prohibit its
use](https://www.cambridgema.gov/-/media/Files/policedepartment/Policies/bodycamerapolicy419.pdf)
due to privacy and surveillance concerns.

ICE uses [facial recognition
technology](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/technology/tech-ice-facial-
recognition-palantir.html) during immigration enforcement operations, but in
2020 lawmakers [raised concerns that body camera facial
recognition](https://doi.org/10.1017/err.2025.26) could dissuade citizens from
protesting out of fear of retribution.

As [protests against ICE immigration
enforcement](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/16/cities-anti-ice-
tactics) continue, it’s known that the agency uses [facial recognition
technology](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/technology/tech-ice-facial-
recognition-palantir.html) on peaceful protesters and observers. Existing ICE
policy prevents the use of facial recognition on “live BWC recordings,”
meaning while the interaction is taking place. Facial recognition is permitted
on body camera footage after the interaction has concluded.

In early February 2026, Democratic lawmakers introduced a measure that would
[prohibit the use of facial
recognition](https://jayapal.house.gov/2026/02/05/markey-jayapal-merkley-
wyden-introduce-bill-to-ban-ice-and-cbp-use-of-facial-recognition-technology-
amid-trumps-rapidly-growing-surveillance-state/) by ICE and CBP agents. That
ban would extend to [facial recognition features on body
cameras](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/07/democrats-fear-body-cameras-
could-be-ices-new-mass-surveillance-tool-00769363).

**Policy compliance**

Policy is only as strong as its enforcement.

Policymakers could consider strengthening submission forms for ICE use-of-
force and [civil rights violation complaints](https://www.dhs.gov/file-civil-
rights-complaint).

Thorough investigation of complaints and reviews of body camera footage could
be handled by an [external review
board](https://www.usccr.gov/files/pubs/sac/wv0104/ch4.htm). The [Office of
the Inspector General](https://oig.justice.gov/), responsible for
investigating allegations of excessive force by ICE agents, could also conduct
reviews.

Body cameras will not deter violence committed by ICE agents unless policies
clearly dictate their use. For body cameras to function as transparency and
accountability tools, I believe wrongdoing would have to be swiftly and
consistently penalized. This would highlight the consequences of noncompliance
with body-worn camera policies.![The
